title: Paris-Brest
subtitle: choux pastry ring filled with hazelnut praline cream
excerpt: Paris-Brest is a French choux ring split and filled with praline mousseline cream. You get crisp pastry, a rich and nutty cream, and a dramatic cut cross-section. Watch the oven: choux must be fully dried out before you open the door or the ring will collapse.
sourceNotes: Classic French patisserie tradition codified in Escoffier (Le Guide Culinaire, 1903) and Careme (works in public domain). The Paris-Brest was created in 1910 by patissier Louis Durand, commissioned to celebrate the Paris to Brest cycling race (public domain history).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Bake the choux ring up to 6 hours ahead and keep uncovered at room temperature. Make the pastry cream and praline up to 24 hours ahead, refrigerating both separately. Assemble within 2 hours of serving.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius. Reduce to 180 degrees Celsius after 15 minutes. Fan oven: start at 185 degrees Celsius, reduce to 165 degrees Celsius after 15 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A cooked paste made by beating flour into boiling butter and water, then incorporating eggs. The high moisture content creates steam during baking, which puffs the pastry into a hollow shell. Choux must be baked thoroughly and dried out fully or it will soften and sink when it cools.

Pastry cream (creme patissiere) beaten with softened butter to create a lighter, richer filling. The butter and pastry cream must be at the same temperature when combined, ideally around 20 degrees Celsius. If one is colder, the mixture splits into a greasy, curdled mess.

Caramelised sugar poured over toasted nuts, then ground to a paste or left as a brittle. Hazelnut praline is the classic filling for Paris-Brest. The caramel must reach a deep amber colour (around 175 degrees Celsius) for full flavour; pale caramel tastes raw and sweet without the bittersweet depth.

content.text: Paris-Brest is a
choux pastry
ring, baked until completely hollow and crisp, then split and filled with hazelnut
praline
mousseline
cream.
You get a ring with shatteringly crisp pastry walls, a cream that is richer than whipped cream but lighter than buttercream, and a hazelnut caramel flavour running through every bite.

Watch the choux ring during baking: do not open the oven before 30 minutes or the steam inside the pastry will escape and the ring will sink; it must be a deep golden brown and feel completely firm before it comes out.
Ingredients
Choux pastry
Hazelnut praline
Mousseline cream
Method
Making the choux paste

Put the water, milk, butter, sugar, and salt into a medium saucepan over medium heat. Stir occasionally until the butter has melted completely, then increase the heat and bring the mixture to a full rolling boil.

Remove the pan from the heat and tip in all the sifted flour at once. Beat vigorously with a wooden spoon until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pan and forms a smooth, cohesive ball. This takes about 1 minute of hard beating. Return the pan to low heat and cook for a further 2 minutes, stirring constantly, to dry out the paste slightly. The paste is ready when a thin film forms on the base of the pan and the paste no longer smells raw.

Tip the paste into a large mixing bowl and leave to cool for 5 minutes. The paste must not be so hot that it scrambles the eggs when you add them. Beat the 4 eggs together in a jug. Add the beaten egg a little at a time, beating well between each addition with a wooden spoon or a stand mixer fitted with the paddle attachment. The final paste should be glossy, smooth, and fall from the spoon in a thick V-shape. You may not need all the egg; stop when the paste reaches this consistency. If the paste is too stiff it will not pipe cleanly; if it is too loose it will spread rather than hold its shape.
Piping the ring

Heat the oven to 200 degrees Celsius (conventional). Line a baking tray with a baking mat or parchment paper. Draw a circle approximately 22 cm in diameter on the underside of the paper using a plate or cake tin as a guide. This is the template for your ring.

Fit a piping bag with a 1.5 cm plain or star tip. Fill with the choux paste. Pipe one ring of choux, following the drawn circle. Pipe a second ring immediately inside the first, touching it. Pipe a third ring on top of the join between the first two rings. This three-ring structure gives the baked ring enough height and wall thickness to support the filling without collapsing when split. If you have spare paste, pipe a few small rounds beside the ring to use as taste tests.
Scatter a few roughly chopped hazelnuts across the top of the piped ring. Press them in very lightly. These give a visual cue to the filling inside and add texture to the crust.
Baking and drying

Place the tray in the preheated oven. Bake at 200 degrees Celsius for 15 minutes, then reduce the heat to 180 degrees Celsius without opening the door and bake for a further 20 minutes. The total bake is 35 minutes. Do not open the oven door during the first 30 minutes: the ring is hollow because of trapped steam, and opening the door releases it before the pastry shell has set, causing the ring to sink.

After 35 minutes, the ring should be a deep golden brown all over and feel completely firm when tapped. If it still feels soft at any point, return it to the oven for 5 minutes more. When baked, turn off the oven, prop the door ajar with a wooden spoon, and leave the ring inside for a further 10 minutes to dry out completely. Transfer to a cooling rack and cool fully before splitting.
Making the praline
Line a baking tray with a silicone mat or oiled foil. Spread the toasted hazelnuts on the tray in a single layer.

Put the caster sugar into a heavy-based saucepan. Set over medium heat and leave undisturbed until the edges begin to melt. Then swirl the pan gently rather than stirring (stirring can cause crystallisation). Cook until all the sugar has melted and the caramel is a deep amber. A sugar thermometer should read around 175 degrees Celsius. At this point the caramel smells nutty and slightly bitter; paler caramel lacks depth.

Pour the hot caramel immediately over the hazelnuts. Leave to cool completely and set hard, about 20 minutes. Break the brittle into rough pieces, then transfer to a food processor and blitz to a fine crumb. Continue blitzing for 3 to 4 minutes until the mixture becomes a smooth, oily paste. This is praline paste. Transfer to a bowl and set aside.
Making the pastry cream
Whisk the egg yolks, caster sugar, and cornflour in a large mixing bowl until smooth and pale. The mixture should form a thick ribbon when the whisk is lifted.

Heat the milk in a medium saucepan over medium heat until steaming and small bubbles form at the edges. Do not boil. Pour about a third of the hot milk onto the yolk mixture, whisking constantly. This tempers the eggs so they do not scramble. Pour the tempered mixture back into the saucepan with the remaining milk.

Return the saucepan to medium heat and cook, stirring constantly with a balloon whisk or silicone spatula, until the cream thickens and large bubbles start to burst through the surface. Keep stirring for a full 2 minutes after the first bubble appears to cook out the cornflour completely; under-cooked pastry cream has a starchy taste and a loose texture that will not support the butter later.
Scrape the hot pastry cream into a bowl. Press a sheet of cling film directly onto the surface to prevent a skin forming. Refrigerate until completely cold, at least 1 hour.
Making the mousseline cream
Remove the cold pastry cream from the refrigerator and beat it firmly until completely smooth and lump-free. If using a stand mixer, use the paddle attachment on medium speed for about 2 minutes.

The butter and the pastry cream must be at the same temperature before combining: ideally around 18 to 20 degrees Celsius. If the pastry cream is colder, the butter will seize and the cream will split into greasy lumps. If the butter is warmer than the pastry cream, the mixture will look curdled and loose. Check both are at room temperature before proceeding.

Add the softened butter to the pastry cream a tablespoon at a time, beating continuously. The mixture will look curdled at around the halfway point; this is normal. Keep adding butter and beating and it will suddenly come together into a light, fluffy, glossy cream.

Add the praline paste and beat until evenly combined. Taste: the cream should be intensely hazelnut, caramel, and rich. Transfer to a piping bag fitted with a large star tip and refrigerate for 20 minutes to firm slightly before piping.
Assembly

Using a long serrated knife, split the cooled choux ring horizontally through its equator. Lift off the top half and set it aside. The inside of the ring should be mostly hollow with some soft, slightly damp pastry in the centre. Pull out any large soft pieces from the interior of both halves: this creates space for more cream and ensures the pastry does not go soggy.

Dust the cut surface of the bottom half lightly with icing sugar. Pipe generous rosettes or tall swirls of the praline mousseline all around the ring, filling it completely and building up above the cut edge. Aim for height: the cream should be clearly visible from the side when the lid is replaced.

Carefully place the top half of the ring back over the cream. Dust generously with icing sugar. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes before serving to allow the cream to firm and the pastry to absorb a little of the cream's moisture. Serve within 2 hours of assembly: the pastry begins to soften as it stands.

attrs.problem: The choux ring sank in the middle after coming out of the oven
attrs.avoid: Avoid opening the oven door before 30 minutes. Steam trapped inside the pastry is what creates the hollow structure; releasing it early causes the soft walls to collapse inward.
attrs.fix: The ring was underbaked. It must be completely firm to the touch and a deep golden colour all over before removal. If in doubt, leave it in the switched-off oven with the door propped ajar for an extra 10 minutes.

attrs.problem: The mousseline cream split into a greasy, curdled texture
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding cold butter to warm pastry cream, or soft butter to cold pastry cream. The temperature difference between the two components is the most common cause of splitting.
attrs.fix: If the cream splits, gently warm the outside of the bowl with your hands or set it briefly over a bowl of warm (not hot) water and beat again. In most cases the cream will come back together as the temperatures equalise.

attrs.problem: The caramel crystallised and turned grainy rather than becoming a clear amber liquid
attrs.avoid: Avoid stirring the caramel once the sugar has started to melt. Movement encourages sugar crystals to form. Swirl the pan gently instead.
attrs.fix: Start again. Crystallised caramel cannot be rescued. Before making the caramel, brush the inside of the pan with a pastry brush dipped in water to wash down any sugar crystals clinging to the sides.

attrs.problem: The choux paste is too stiff to pipe smoothly
attrs.avoid: Avoid adding all the beaten egg at once. The amount of egg needed varies with the moisture content of the flour and how long the paste was dried out over heat.
attrs.fix: Beat in a little extra beaten egg, a teaspoon at a time, until the paste reaches the correct consistency: smooth, glossy, and dropping in a thick, slow V-shape from the spoon.

attrs.problem: The pastry cream has a starchy, floury taste
attrs.avoid: Avoid removing the pan from the heat as soon as the cream thickens. Cornflour needs to cook for at least 2 full minutes at bubbling temperature to lose its raw starch flavour.
attrs.fix: If the cream has already set cold and tastes starchy, it cannot be fixed after the fact. Next time, keep the cream at a vigorous simmer for a full 2 minutes after the first bubble appears, stirring constantly.

content.text: The correct consistency for
choux pastry

is described as a V-shape: lift a spoonful and let it fall back. The paste should hang for a moment in a thick ribbon, then fall cleanly, leaving the spoon with a pointed V of paste. Too stiff and the paste will not pipe evenly; too loose and the piped ring will spread flat in the oven.
